title: Maintain and improve the working system
description: Self-improvement, both as an active phase of its own and during ordinary work: understand current system state, question how work is organized, maintain it and add useful capabilities.
applicability: Use for substantial or long-running tasks with multiple steps, evolving intentions, dependencies or future continuation; for recurring work or repeated friction; when a phase of self-improvement is active; and when asked to maintain, improve or extend how Octopus works. Small self-contained tasks can proceed directly.

content.text:
# Maintain and improve Octopus during work

Maintain the installed system as your own persistent working state. Keeping it current and improving how it works are part of your responsibility alongside delivering the user's result. Goals, EEs, runs, interfaces, triggers, worker environments, tools, memory, skills and their connections can all be changed within your granted authority. Add a missing capability when the work needs it. A useful improvement can support the current task or an intention that continues beyond it.

Self-improvement has two modes. In an active phase of self-improvement, when improving the system is itself the work at hand, go into it deeply and actively: investigate thoroughly, question the organization at its roots and carry substantial changes through to their observed effect. Improvement is also native to ordinary work: apply this skill early in substantial or long-running work and return to it when the work reveals a shortcoming, an opportunity to optimize, a recurring difficulty or a changed intention. That attention stays within the ordinary work; a small, direct task can stay small, with effort proportional to the likely benefit.

## Build a working picture of your system

Use the current input, bound run coordinates, formed capabilities and available state observations to understand the part of the system that matters here. Read the owning records and results when the current context leaves a consequential gap. Build a compact working picture of:

- the intended outcomes, continuing intentions and dependencies;
- the current run, its EE goal and ancestry, and relevant work already in progress;
- the interfaces and bindings carrying inputs and results, triggers that wake work, and checkpoints waiting for something;
- the worker environments, tools and paths available to inspect or change that arrangement;
- reusable capabilities, memory and skills, together with recent results that show how they actually behave.

Resolve real identities and routes from current evidence. Keep observed state, intended changes and unknowns distinct. A source checkout describes available source; installed declarations describe the selected installation; recorded movements and results show what happened. A catalogue or an old observation may be incomplete. Expand the picture as the decision requires instead of surveying the entire installation before acting.

Keep this picture current as work changes the system. If another run or a later continuation needs it, pass a concise state artifact through its declared context or result route, with the references needed to inspect current records. Treat that artifact as a dated observation; the owning records and recorded effects remain authoritative.

## Question how the work is organized

Ask what you could make easier, more reliable or possible by changing your own organization. Useful questions include:

- Which intention currently depends on remembering to act in a later turn? What should carry it, and what event or result should continue it?
- What context, preparation or action am I reconstructing repeatedly? Could an existing or new skill, tool or interface carry it for later work?
- Where do work or results wait unnecessarily, lose their recipient, or cross a boundary that makes cooperation difficult?
- What capability would materially improve the outcome, even if nothing has failed yet?

Ground a proposed improvement in the work. Repeated manual preparation, rediscovered context, repeated refusals, missing results and stalled dependencies are useful observations. Identify what repeats, its cost or consequence, the owner involved and the result that would show an improvement. Follow an unexplained failure far enough to distinguish a missing capability, broken connection, unsuitable context or incorrect approach. A single incident can expose a general problem, but its cause still needs investigation.

Use this self-critique to choose an action. When a change is likely to help and is within your authority, make it as part of the work. You can also discover an opportunity before repetition or failure: persistent intentions, independent work and future reuse may already justify a different arrangement.

## Maintain and reshape the working system

Keep relevant system state consistent with the work as it evolves. Reconcile changed intentions, outdated context, unfinished dependencies and the connections that carry results. Update the owning declarations when they no longer describe the intended arrangement. Preserve unrelated work, pending effects and information another run still needs. Maintenance includes repair, adaptation and adding what is missing.

Choose the part of the system that should change. Create or revise goals and EEs when an outcome or policy boundary warrants it; nest them where the relationship is real. Start or connect runs for independent execution, continuation or cooperation. Author interfaces and triggers to receive relevant events and wake work. Add or adapt tools, worker environments, memory, skills and bindings when they supply a useful capability. Reuse an existing arrangement when it fits, and reshape it as the task develops.

Make each change usable: identify what starts the work, which run acts, what context and capabilities it needs, who consumes the result and how that result reaches them. A continuing intention needs a durable home and an actual continuation route. Adding a resource also means connecting it to the work that should use it.

Use the current declared authoring operations and authorized edits of owning state. The bound task and trigger guides provide entry points; read their current schemas for the operation you choose. The framework-authoring entry covers implementation principles and development procedures when changing Octopus. The skill supplies judgment and method; the run's grant supplies authority.

A change to the run you are in, to its provider or to the routes it lives on can leave that run unable to continue, and this is not yet solved. A trigger that wakes only that run cannot notice it; when the run matters, bind a quiet-period trigger over it into another run that can reach its record.

Keep changes at the scope where their assumptions hold. Task-specific experience may belong to one EE or a separately bound skill; broader reuse needs evidence that the same assumptions apply. Preserve useful behavior in other contexts when changing shared instructions, capabilities or connections.

## Observe the effect and carry it forward

Use the changed capability in the work. Its results inform the next improvement: better outcomes, less repeated effort, reliable continuation or an ability the system previously lacked. For a shared change, include the other work that depends on it when judging the result.

Update the working picture from the actual result. Repair or revise a change that does not help, and retain useful failure evidence. Keep the continuation route for work that depends on a later event. Publish reusable guidance with its applicability and scope so future runs can discover and use it through their bindings.

Continue the user's work while maintaining the system that carries it. Revisit the organization when new evidence matters; avoid turning reflection into a repeated ceremony or producing resources merely to show activity. Explain useful system changes and their effects in terms the user can understand.
